Bills Core For Following Three Seasons (27-29)
stories.summary:
I run this exercise every so often during the season to take a heat check of what the Bills core more or less looks like like for the next three years. This is based off current play, odds of being on the roster in those years, and areas that feel most stable vs not. I like doing this to see where the holes are that the team may target to improve. Here we go:



	 



	Offense: 



	QB: Josh



	RB: Cook



	WR: Moore, Shakir



	OL: Dion Dawkins, O'Cyrus Torrence, Spencer Brown



	TE: Dalton Kincaid



	 



	Locks: Josh, James Cook, O'Cyrus Torrence, Spencer Brown



	Expect Them Here Outside Of Major Contract Move: DJ Moore, Khalil Shakir, Dion Dawkins, Dalton Kincaid



	 



	The offense is probably the best overall its been with Josh so that piece is easier so that is certainly more a maintenance piece then full scale changes. Connor McGovern has three years left, but his dead cap is just 5.5 in 2029 with a cap hit of 17.7 mil and I can see the Bills lining up a replacement or cutting him for cap as he would be 32. Alec Anderson is a FA and a position where they could extend or draft to get younger and save a little more money. Keon Coleman has one year left on his contract and while he has finally emerged into a quality WR-3, I can see the Bills targeting a youngster or two this draft or next to backload for him walking and Moore aging over the next three years. Dawson Knox has regressed this year both catching and blocking and that contract is eventually going to get him in the next year or two. Again they can get younger and cheaper for similar production.



	 



	Defense:



	LDE: TJ Sanders backup Landon Jackson



	NT: Deone Walker 



	LB: Greg Rousseau - Kaleb Elarms-Orr - TJ Parker



	Corner: Benford - IGB - Jordan Hancock



	Safety Bishop - Hooker



	 



	The defense has some areas of strength but I am expecting more resources for at least this next draft to really shore up areas like LB, NCB, and a bit more at the NT/DE area. Ed Oliver's contract ends in 2028 and that year he has a 10.8 mil dead cap. There is a void year available where they could lower his hit with an extension, but I also wouldn't be surprised if he is traded to a rebuilding team for a mid round pick. The talent is there but the availability is a killer. Terrel Bernard's dead cap drops to 6.45 in 2028 and 3.9 mil in 2027. They may keep him for another year but draft a guy to takeover once that dead cap drops. He just doesn't match the scheme and injuries have killed any potential he flashed. Dorian Williams is a free agent after this season and maybe they keep him for cheap for a year or two, but he is rotation at best.



	 



	Between IGB's development & Hookers addition I feel the secondary is turning into a true area of strength and if they can find a true NCB it could be downright scary. The Bills have pieces at the line region to work with, more depth or a better running mate for Rousseau would really elevate that area even more. The middle LB spot though with Bernard & Williams is the area you could truly makeover. KEO has shown a few flashes maybe he turns into the guy we all hope. But you can absolutely upgrade there with someone younger.

stories.title: The Blackhawks’ Rebuild Is Giving Sabres Fans Flashbacks to 2015
stories.summary:
For Buffalo Sabres fans, something feels familiar about watching the Chicago Blackhawks build around Connor Bedard. The young star arrives. The franchise has a new face. Suddenly, years of losing feel easier to justify because someone might make the wait worthwhile. After they played each other on November 12th, that Blackhawks team reminded me a lot of the early Eichel years.



Rebuilds get complicated. The roster still has holes. Injuries interrupt the progress. The conversation shifts from what the young star can become to how much longer he will have to wait for a winning team. Buffalo lived through that after drafting Jack Eichel. Chicago should be paying attention.



Buffalo selected Eichel second overall in 2015; Chicago took Bedard first overall in 2023. Their arrivals gave both fan bases a reason to look beyond the standings. Getting that player is an enormous achievement, but it also changes expectations for everyone building around him.



Mar 13, 2025; Columbus, Ohio, USA; Vegas Golden Knights center Jack Eichel (9) controls the puck against the Columbus Blue Jackets during the third period at Nationwide Arena. Mandatory Credit: Russell LaBounty-Imagn Images



The Sabres acquired Ryan O’Reilly, Evander Kane and Robin Lehner in 2015. On paper, there was a case for believing the next competitive Buffalo team was taking shape. Eichel would be its centerpiece, surrounded by players expected to help move the organization forward. That is the stage of a rebuild where potential can become misleading. A promising collection of names still needs to become a team that can defend, generate offense beyond its best line, and survive an injury.



Bedard and Eichel make a useful comparison because both produced before their teams became competitive. Eichel recorded 56 points in 81 games as a rookie; Bedard had 61 in 68. Those totals came in different scoring environments and should not settle an argument about their ceilings. They do show that neither player needed years to begin contributing.



Bedard followed that with 75 points in 69 games in 2025–26. His development as an offensive player gives Chicago something substantial to build around. The challenge is turning his production into team progress. That is where the injuries make the Buffalo comparison especially uncomfortable. Eichel’s major early injury interruptions came after his rookie season. A high ankle sprain cost him the first 21 games of 2016–17; another cost him 15 games in 2017–18. He was definitely not the same skater when he came back.



Nov 21, 2025; Buffalo, New York, USA; Chicago Blackhawks center Connor Bedard (98) controls the puck from Buffalo Sabres defenseman Mattias Samuelsson (23) in the first period at KeyBank Center. Mandatory Credit: Mark Konezny-Imagn Images



Bedard missed 14 games with a fractured jaw as a rookie, then 12 following a right shoulder injury last season. This summer brought surgery on his left shoulder. He returned for his season debut on October 13, ahead of the original November projection.



These are different injuries, involving different body parts and recovery periods. The similarity is what those absences can do to a developing team. Buffalo had a little more depth back then, but it still led to losing records and frustrated teammates. With Chicago, Bedard was more of a one-person show, and without him the team struggled to score.



A young center needs repetitions with his linemates. A power play needs time together. Coaches need to learn which combinations work. When the player at the center of the plan disappears from the lineup, those answers become harder to find. Their return can also create an unreasonable expectation: now that the star is healthy, everything should improve immediately. Blackhawks coach Jeff Blashill addressed that when Bedard returned, saying, “We can’t expect him to put the puzzle together by himself.”



Buffalo fans should recognize the problem behind that sentence. A franchise center can improve a lineup considerably. He still needs teammates who can move the puck up ice, finish chances, and keep games manageable when he is on the bench.



Chicago has Patrick Kane and Bowen Byram alongside a young core that includes Frank Nazar, Anton Frondell, Alex Vlasic, and Artyom Levshunov. There are players worth developing and reasons to believe the roster can improve. The next step is getting enough of them to become dependable NHL contributors at the same time.



For Chicago, the lesson from Buffalo is to judge the entire roster honestly. Bedard’s scoring cannot become the main evidence that everything else is working. Improvement should also show up in the team’s ability to create offense without him, defend consistently, and remain competitive when important players are unavailable. Both also signed big second contracts which, while deserved, definitely made fans think they can save the team single-handedly.



There is also a limit to the injury comparison. Eichel’s 2021 neck injury brought a public disagreement with Buffalo over his surgical treatment. He was traded to Vegas that November. That conflict belongs to a much later chapter of his Buffalo career; it should not be projected onto Bedard simply because he has missed games.



Eichel never reached the playoffs with Buffalo, then won the Stanley Cup with Vegas in 2023. To me, that is the most useful warning for Chicago: an organization can identify a franchise player correctly and still fail to build a successful team around him. Connor McDavid is the best player in the world, hockey is a team sport, and it takes a well-rounded team to win the Stanley Cup.



The Blackhawks are not guaranteed to repeat Buffalo’s experience. Their decisions from here will determine whether the resemblance becomes stronger or fades. But Sabres fans remember what 2015 felt like. The hardest part seemed finished because the franchise center had finally arrived. Chicago has reached the point where it must prove the rest of the rebuild can catch up to its best player. Rebuilds do not follow a positive linear rate, and not all the draft picks you made from acquired picks will make the team. Sometimes you need resets within the rebuild, but don’t let your star player stay frustrated for long; it is almost impossible to find those types of players outside of drafting them.

Does teams get better at defending tush push after 6 years?
stories.summary:
I saw Winston's "who let the dogs out" 4th and 1 fake last night. And people are mentioning how Josh does it with automatic success rate. But I do notice that it is getting harder the way I see from the Bills.



	 



	If i remember correctly, it was Belichick and Tom Brady started the idea of plunging the middle for inches almost 10 years ago. At that time, it is more about cadence to maximize the fact O-Line's advantage of knowing the snap count to get a jump on D Line. Very successful indeed. Then around 2020, The Eagles' Hurts and Kelce were able to execute the tush push more of a brute force version. Great Center and an athletic, running back bodied QB who finds a gap, then letting guys behind push him into the gap for a yard.



	 



	McDermott adopted that into the Bills, using Allen's athleticism. And it seems like the Bills are the main team who are still doing it consistently. But opposing Defenses are not just giving up. They have studied that play of the Bills and have come up with a few stops along the way. To me, it is not automatic like I used to feel, against a stout defense. The Vikings game is such an example that it took 2 tries and a reply reversal to convert.



	 



	The Bills have the personnel to execute the play. But variation is hard because they don't have, say a big strong half/full back with short yardage vision, to allow Allen to hand off in those situations.

stories.title: Sabres Can’t Close It Out, Fall to Blackhawks 3–2 in Overtime
stories.summary:
Boxscore



Score: Buffalo Sabres 2–3 Chicago Blackhawks (OT)Shots: BUF 23–25 CHIBuffalo Sabres Goals: Power (Norris, Quinn); Thompson PPG (Quinn, Dahlin)Chicago Blackhawks Goals: Nazar PPG (Bedard, Kantserov); Nazar (Rinzel, Moore); Donato (Frondell, Rinzel).



Quick Thoughts



A Good Start on the Road



After giving up eight to Tampa Bay the night before, the Sabres needed a good first period in Chicago. They got one. Owen Power opened the scoring nine minutes in with a slap shot from the circle. Frank Nazar tied it from in close on the power play, but Tage Thompson answered with a wrister from the circle on Buffalo’s own man advantage. Jack Quinn assisted on both Sabres goals, and Buffalo took a 2–1 lead into the intermission.



Where Was the Third Goal?



Buffalo outshot Chicago 10–6 in the second, but Spencer Knight kept it a one-goal game. That was the period where the Sabres had their best chance to put some distance between themselves and the Blackhawks. Instead, they went into the third still asking two first-period goals to hold up.



Chicago made them pay at 8:22 of the third. Nazar got his stick on the puck in the slot and redirected it past Alex Lyon for his second of the night. Buffalo had a power play less than two minutes later and couldn’t regain the lead. The Sabres finished 1-for-4 on the man advantage. They got one when they needed it in the first and could’ve used another right there.



Donato Gets the Last Word



Ryan Donato scored from the high slot 3:12 into overtime to give Chicago the win. Lyon finished with 22 saves, and Knight stopped 21, including every Buffalo shot after Thompson’s goal. Chicago snapped a six-game skid. Buffalo’s losing streak is now three.



At The Horn



A point on the second night of a back-to-back is useful. It still feels like Buffalo left one in Chicago. The Sabres got a goal from Power, a power-play goal from Thompson, and two assists from Quinn. They had the lead after 40 minutes. What they didn’t get was another goal over the final 47 minutes. There are too many passengers in each game lately. This team’s strength was depth last year, but it hasn’t shown up yet. The Sabres were in a worse position at this time last year before they went on a run, but that’s what makes it more frustrating, knowing that this team is better. A lot of players had career years last year, and while that can’t happen every year, only Power, Benson, Quinn, and Ostlund have improved; Tage and Samuelsson are what they should be, but the rest have regressed. Being in the toughest division makes it worse when they lose games they had the lead in.



Next up is Dallas on Saturday at 8 p.m. ET, the second stop on the six-game road trip. If Buffalo takes another lead into the third, I’d like to see them spend more of it looking for the next goal.

Game #19 Preview & Open Thread: Buffalo Sabres at Chicago Blackhawks
stories.summary:
It’s the Second Night of Back to Back Games for Buffalo



Buffalo Sabres (8-7-3) vs Chicago Blackhawks (4-13-1)



Puck Drop: 8:00 pm ET | United Center



TV: MSG-B, DAZN, ESPN+ (Hulu), NHL Center Ice



Radio: WGR 550, Sirius XM (app)



Know Your Opponent



Chicago Blackhawks



Record: 4-13-1 | 9 PTS



Last Game: Lost a heartbreaker 9-2 to Carolina



Division Ranking: 8th in Central



PP: 9.8% 32nd (Sabres 15.3% 29th)



PK: 78.6% 12th (Sabres 69.8% 26th)



Season Series: Buffalo rallied to beat the Blackhawks 4-3 earlier in the season.



What to Watch



1. Horrendous Homestand is Thankfully Over



Buffalo came home last week to begin a four-game homestand following a successful four-game road trip, where they collected seven of a possible eight points. Unfortunately, instead of building on that momentum, the Sabres laid a 1-3 egg in four straight starts at KeyBank Center. Six valuable points slipped away, with four of them going to division rivals. Lindy Ruff’s team just can’t seem to get it done in their own barn right now, dating back to last season’s playoff run. Buffalo is 4-6-0 at home this year after a 2-5 record in the 2026 postseason. Total it up and the Sabres only have six wins in their last 17 contests at Keybank. That’s a troubling trend, for sure.



The same familiar issues continue to haunt this team. The defense is giving up far too many quality scoring opportunities, the goaltending isn’t coming up with the big saves when needed, and the offense is struggling to put the puck in the net. Meanwhile, the special teams have been downright awful. In other words, just about every part of this team has something to answer for. Perhaps another road trip is exactly what the Sabres need to regroup and get themselves back on track. Three recent regulation losses, all at home, have put a dent in their standings position and allowed the gaps between them and division rivals to widen.



Tonight’s opponent, Chicago, comes in as the second-worst team in the league. But honestly, that almost doesn’t matter given the way Buffalo has been playing. The Sabres need a complete, top-to-bottom effort and, more importantly, a winning result. Last night’s deflating performance against Tampa Bay was unacceptable, especially after Buffalo fought its way back into the game to make it a one-goal contest at 4-3. That comeback ultimately went for nothing, as the team got blown the hell out after that, falling 8-3.



After that humbling performance on national television, every player in that locker room needs to take a long look in the mirror. This team has dug itself into a hole, and it’s time to start climbing out.



2. No on Bo Again



Former Sabre Bo Byram remains sidelined and will miss both matchups against his former team this season. Byram last appeared for the Blackhawks on October 13 and was initially listed as day-to-day before being placed on injured reserve retroactive to October 15. He remains day-to-day, and the saga surrounding his injury and availability in Chicago continues.



Reports have varied regarding whether Byram has received baseline medical clearance, but both his camp and the coaching staff have indicated that he has yet to regain full physical comfort level. He has been limited to non-contact participation in practice.



So far, the blockbuster trade that brought the former Sabres defenseman to Chicago hasn’t exactly worked out as planned. Between the mysterious nature of his “comfort level” injury and his underwhelming play when healthy enough to get into the lineup, Byram has struggled to make an impact. He has managed just one assist in six games with Chicago while posting a troubling minus-7 rating.







3. Need to be Better



The Sabres need to start stringing together some wins, and they need to do it now. The teams ahead of them in the Atlantic Division are doing Buffalo no favors. Boston, Montreal, Tampa Bay, Ottawa and Florida have all been winning regularly or at least picking up valuable loser points. Buffalo can’t afford to keep falling behind.



The Sabres are playing the second half of a back-to-back, but they are the far superior team on paper. No excuses here. If Buffalo wants to keep pace in the division, this is a game they absolutely need to win.



Meanwhile, the Blackhawks come into this one well-rested, having been off since Saturday’s embarrassing 9-2 drubbing at the hands of the Carolina Hurricanes. They’ve had five days to stew over that performance, and you can bet they’ll be looking to make a statement early. Expect Chicago to come out pressing and looking to put Buffalo on its heels right from the opening puck drop.



News and Notes:



The Sabres did not hold a morning skate today, meaning we’ll have to wait until warmups for any lineup changes.



Alex Lyon is expected to make his season debut at some point during Buffalo’s upcoming six-game road trip. Lyon has yet to appear in a game this season, but appears to be nearing a return. Head coach Lindy Ruff offered an encouraging update, saying, “He’s on target to join us, for sure, soon here.” His return would give the Sabres another option in goal and provide some much-needed support to the goaltending rotation as the team hits the road.



Sabre-killer Patrick Kane is out for Chicago. Kane was placed on injured reserve with an upper-body injury on November 9th and remains out for tonight’s matchup.



Buffalo has won seven consecutive games against the Blackhawks, so let’s hope the Sabres can keep that streak alive tonight.

stories.title: I Think We're Seeing the Effects of the Coaching Change
stories.summary:
I've been writing about this for a couple of weeks now. The Vikings game reminded me again. 



	 



	I think we're seeing a changed team this season, and I think it's because of the coaching.



	 



	I think McDermott's mantra was "do your job, be your 1/11th." I think Brady's and Leonhard's mantra is "make a play." It's almost as though McDermott said, "I don't care if you don't make a play, just be in position," and Brady said, "I don't care if you're in position, just make a play."



	 



	It's the phrase we hear all the time: "He's a player's coach."



	 



	Where do I see it?  All over, but mostly on defense. For example:



	 



	Groot's made more plays in 8 games than in any full season since he's joined the team.



	 



	Williams. I'm just speculating here, but I wonder if Williams was always a step slow because he was intent on doing his job. Now it looks like he's just playing. His coverage on the interception was a case in point. He can run with almost anyone. 



	 



	Chubb. Watch the mic'd up from the Vikings game. He's running around the field, chattering away, always light-hearted, always positive, having fun. Very un-McDermott-like. 



	 



	There was something about their attitude on Monday night, too. They went three and out for -11 yards, but there didn't seem to be any panic. It was just, "okay, we'll figure this out." They get sending Cook into brick walls, but you could see that the openings that Cook ordinarily exploits were almost but not quite there, so they just kept working at it. I had the sense that Brady just kept trying things, poking around, feeling for the openings to take advantage of.  Something about the effort throughout the entire first half said, "We got this." 



	 



	And, still, we haven't seen their best football. The defense, for sure, has more in store, particularly with the addition of Hooker. Tyrell Shavers will be back soon, and he's a good bet to make a play here or there. And Brady just keep inventing and installing new stuff, week after week. 



	 



	I think we're seeing a different team. In particular, I think we're seeing a coaching program that is building the team toward the best version of itself, and even the coaches can't tell us today what it will look like in January. Under the old regime, what we saw was a team that installed an offense and a defense in training camp and then spent the season trying to perfect it. That system made the Bills more and more predictable as the season went on. This team, this season, doesn't seem predictable at all. They just keep getting better.

stories.title: Sabres fried by Lightning for second straight spanking
stories.summary:
Buffalo almost came from behind again, but then Kucherov took over



Boxscore



Score: Buffalo Sabres 3-8 Tampa Bay LightningShots: BUF 31-22 TBL



Buffalo Sabres Goals: Doan 4 PPG (McLeod, Norris), Zucker 2 (Östlund, Quinn), Thompson 11 (Krebs, Samuelsson)Tampa Bay Lightning Goals: Sabourin 1 (Geekie, Guentzel), Carlson 6 PPG (Guentzel, D’Astous), Hagel 10 (Cirelli, Carlson), Gourde 1 (Guentzel, O’Reilly), Kucherov 6 (Hagel, Carlson), Kucherov 7 (Carlson, Cirelli), Kucherov 8 PPG (Carlson, Guentzel), Hagel 11 (Kucherov, Cirelli)



Quick Thoughts



Folks, not going to go to great lengths to explain that we were beaten comprehensively tonight by a savvy, experienced team. 



The Sabres were actually even in this one for most of the first period before an irresponsible backcheck allowed the Bolts to go up by one following a Ukko Pekka Luukkonen save on an odd-man rush. It got worse as Josh Doan took an ill-timed delay of game penalty just seconds later and the penalty kill was so inept that the old fossil John Carlson had enough time to fan on his first attempt, corral the puck and still beat UPL coming across to make it 2-0 just before the first period ended, and it took them only sixteen seconds on the power play. 



Buffalo has been atrocious with their shooting percentage at home (as Adam pointed out in the preview), and that luck did not change tonight. Tampa then gleefully took advantage when the Sabres didn’t clear out the space in front of UPL and the unsighted goalie didn’t even see the third go in, before more lazy backchecking resulted in an odd-man rush that made it 4-0 just past the halfway mark in this game.



Coming just days after they were outgunned 4-1 by Vegas Golden Knights, it was incomprehensible that the Sabres could continue to be so poor but yet there it was. However, credit where it’s due, as the Sabres did attempt to mount a comeback. 



The much-maligned power play finally broke a double-digit futility streak albeit it took the second unit to get it done, Doan tapping in the puck to make it 4-1. With the period winding down then Noah Östlund got a lovely return pass from Jack Quinn to get in space and he fed an open Jason Zucker to scoop home and make it 4-2. 



The third period started with aplomb as the Sabres smelled a comeback. The arena was soon rocking as Tage ‘TNT’ Thompson finally woke up. Ultimate wingman Peyton Krebs drove into the Tampa zone, turned around and passed back for Tage to crank one in off the far pipe and it was 4-3. 



The Sabres threw the kitchen sink at the Bolts for the next minute and came this close to leveling things but veteran goaltender Andrei Vasilevskiy made the right saves at the right time and before you know it, league MVP Nikita Kucherov suddenly showed up in a big way with a hat-trick to take the game away from the Sabres. After Kuch had potted on the odd-man rush to make it 5-3 Lindy Ruff decided enough was enough with UPL and threw on Colten Ellis. If his hope was the move would jolt the Sabres, it didn’t work. 



Brandon Hagel even had time to add an eighth for good measure with five to play, and aforementioned fossil Carlson ended the night with five points on a goal and four assists, 8-3 the final score.   



At The Horn



Buffalo continues to beat themselves this season when they’re not committing to playing team defense. They’re seeing themselves get found out by smart hockey teams with skilled veterans who know how to catch them out, and while you can blame the Sabres goaltending to some extent, they’re not helping themselves with poor backchecking. Sitting non-performing players hasn’t been working out either, so we’re all curious to see what Lindy Ruff tries next. 



The Sabres are 4-6-0 at home and 4-1-3 on the road, but that also includes three road games against three spectacularly inept California teams so who knows what they’ll manage on their upcoming six-game road trip.

Micheal Hoechtamalu jumping the LOS at the snap and trying to intercept a spike got me thinking
stories.summary:
There might be something here that the Bills could practice and put in their back pocket for a key moment late in a playoff game that could actually foul up an opposing offense if they execute it well and nobody is expecting it.



	First off, Hoecht can't try it again the rest of the season; it needs to be completely forgotten so nobody even considers prepping for it. Secondly, forget about him actually intercepting the ball. With him diving forward and landing face first with his arms fully extended, there is no way he can be in enough control of this hands to actually gather a ball that is coming straight down with any velocity whatsoever.



	However what he could do if he could get himself into that position again is to try to tip the ball back up into the air to create chaos and confusion for a QB that is not expecting it. It doesn't have to go 10' in the air, even getting it 5-6' up there is all you'd really need. You have a specific call for it ready for a specific instance and in addition to Hoecht's role, you also have both Ends crashing hard into the A gaps against an interior OL that is not expecting it with their only job being to get as much push as they possibly can within the first second and create traffic and stress the QB. Then behind them you have Bernard driving hard across the LOS, completely ignoring any offensive players and solely focused on only one thing, getting his hands on a ball that is floating around in the middle of mayhem.



	There are 4 probable scenarios that are likely to result if Hoecht manages to get in position and tip the ball up. 3 of the 4 are positives for the Bills at a huge moment late in the game.



	 



	#1- The Ends get little to no push and a smart QB instinctively bats the ball right back down



	Advantage: Nobody - It just turns out to be the spike play they were already running.



	 



	#2- The Ends do get some push and a tired QB who's unprepared for the situation makes the mistake of instinctively catching the ball to protect it. He panics and just tries to spike it again, which is a penalty for an illegal forward pass because he's already thrown it once.



	Advantage: Bills - The offense loses the down, also loses the yardage on the penalty and there is also possibly (probably?) a clock runoff because of the nature of the offensive penalty with less than 2:00 left.



	 



	#3- The Ends do get some push and a tired QB who's unprepared for the situation makes the mistake of instinctively catching the ball to protect it. Instead of trying to spike it again he realizes he can't, but with no blocking called and nobody out on routes, he likely just takes a quick sack.



	Huge advantage: Bills - This puts an offense into a chaotic situation where they can't just quickly call another spike because if they do, it's going to suddenly be 3rd and long with another 10-15 seconds gone. They have got to call a play while they're panicking and stressed in an unexpected situation, which is going to take too much time and is not likely to be effective at all, which again will likely end up with them suddenly in a 3rd/long situation with even more time ahving run off.



	 



	#4- The Ends get good push, the surprised QB can't get through the bodies and Bernard actually gets across the LOS and snatches the ball.



	Game over: Bills advance in the playoffs



	 



	 



	Am I nuts, or is this actually feasible with some practice?



	Or both?-)

stories.title: Mid-Season Highs & Lows
stories.summary:
We are halfway through the season, and our Bills are 7-1 for the first time since 1993.



	Sounds like a reason to celebrate. I thought at best the Bills would be 6-2 at this point, at worst 5-3.



	Joe Brady has answered the call and Josh Allen and the offense are humming right along, it hasn't always been pretty, but when the game is on the line and the Bills need to score, I feel confident that the Bills can score at any moment.



	The defense, as expected, is a work-in-progress. Giving up lots of points early was concerning. Have these last two games shown that the defense is turning things around? We shall see. Especially now that we've added Amani Hooker.



	 



	I wanted to get your thoughts on the highs and lows of the team.



	 



	Highs:



	Tyler Bass. His kicks can still be entertaining, but give this guy credit, he has rebounded in a big way. Bravo, Bass-O-Matic!



	Keon Coleman: He is not a #1 WR, but his play has been tremendous. Little to complain about.



	Greg Rousseau: This is an easy choice, but seeing Groot play the way he has consistently, has been amazing.



	DJ Moore: When he's on the field, he is a difference maker.



	Josh Allen: Another obvious choice, but he is the team, a star. He does make some odd decisions, but when the game is on the line, we can count on him.



	Ty Johnson: He still is a great option as a running back & receiver.



	James Cook: The fumbles have been rough however he is our top runner and he's always giving his all. Watching how shifty he is and how he can break through the line is fantastic.



	Deone Walker & Ed Oliver: They may not get a ton of stats, but they are monsters.



	Christian Benford: Struggled early, but has come back strong after his injury, and is showing why he's our top Cornerback.
	Davison Igbinosun: By far our top rookie. Had some penalty issues, but he looks very comfortable in coverage, and has been a good defender.



	Joe Brady: Some cute and questionable playcalling still happens, but he does play to the strengths of the offense. I also appreciate how he treated James Cook during his fumbling issues. Instead of having him sit on the sidelines for a quarter, he showed how much he trusted him by sending him back out there.



	Starting Offensive Line: Not much to complain about with this group.



	Halftime Adjustments: Whatever they are feeding the team at halftime, keep giving it to them.



	 



	Lows:



	Penalties: Crazy amount early this season. This has to be fixed.



	CJ Gardner-Johnson: I really thought he would be the leader in our secondary.



	Joshua Palmer: I thought we would see a rebound from this guy.



	Michael Hoecht: I guess this is what happens to a player after an achilles injury. Aside from being a Special Teams demon, he's done little.



	Javon Solomon: Yes, he's not a starter, but this is his third season with the team, and all I see is a Special Teamer.



	Jackson Hawes: Penalties have been a killer for him. Definitely has taken a step back.



	 



	That's how I see it. What's your takeaway?

stories.title: Game #18 Preview & Open Thread: Sabres vs. Lightning
stories.summary:
Buffalo, Tampa Bay



Buffalo Sabres (8-6-3) vs. Tampa Bay Lightning (11-4-2)



Puck Drop: 7 p.m. ET | KeyBank Center, Buffalo, N.Y.



TV: TNT/truTV, HBOMaxRadio: WGR 550



Know Your Opponent



Tampa Bay Lightning

Last Game: 4-3 loss at Winnipeg



Division Ranking: 3rd



PP: 22nd, 19.4% [Sabres: 30th, 14.3%]



PK: 24th, 72.9% [Sabres: 26th, 71.2%]



Season Series: Sabres 3-0-1 vs. Lightning in 2025-26 season



What to Watch



1. Fireworks inbound?



As the Sabres and Lightning meet for the first time this season, it’s hard not to think back to (arguably) the greatest regular season Sabres game this decade.



Goals, fights, comebacks and everything in between made last season’s 8-7 Sabres win over Tampa Bay an instant classic, and a crucial game in Buffalo’s march to claim the Atlantic Division. Why not run it back?



“It’s a division game,” forward Zach Benson told Sabres.com. “It’s a big two points. It’s a four-point game early, so it’s always gonna be heated. Those division (games) are always gonna be heated, tough, hard to play against. We’re ready for it, and we’re excited.”



2. McLeod in, Kulich out



After taking a seat for two games, Ryan McLeod is poised to return to the Sabres lineup, taking the place of Jiri Kulich.



The two forwards haven’t met expectations so far this season, with both posting just three points. With Kulich returning from missing nearly an entire season, it’s fair to assume it’ll take some time to find his game and scoring touch, but McLeod’s poor play has been more of a surprise.



McLeod was one of Buffalo’s most consistent forwards a year ago, but has only seemed to be visible for the wrong reasons in this early season. His defensive blunder in last week’s loss to Ottawa allowed the Senators to tie the game late, and may well have been a contributor to his benching.



He is slated to center a line with Josh Doan and Jason Zucker, two other Sabres who have not quite lived up to expectations this season. Time will tell if watching a couple games from the press box helps reinvigorate the 27-year-old. 



3. Home ice scoring struggles



The Sabres have not found their scoring touch at home.



Buffalo ranks 31st in the NHL with an 8.2 shooting percentage at all strengths on home ice, compared to 8th on the road. They have scored 13.64 goals below expected at home, the worst mark in the league.



Buffalo has long been a positive shooting team, which greatly helped them return to the playoffs a year ago. While the Sabres lost some offensive talent in Alex Tuch, it does fully not explain the regression of home-ice scoring, as Buffalo ranked 6th in the NHL in home shooting percentage last season.



The good news for the Sabres, though, is that they are doing the right things to win games at home. Despite their woeful scoring numbers, they have actually been a top 10 team at driving play on home ice with a 54.97 xGF%. 



So, is it the loss of scoring talent? Running into hot goalies? Simply bad luck? Who’s to say. But if the Sabres continue to get the chances they’ve been creating, it’s hard to imagine their finishing will stay this poor.



*All stats courtesy of NaturalStatTrick.



4. A notable debut



The Lightning are set to give their top prospect a shot on NHL ice Wednesday.



Forward Sam O’Reilly was called up from AHL Syracuse in the wake of an injury to Lightning star Brayden Point, and it appears the 20-year-old Toronto native will make his NHL debut against the Sabres.



O’Reilly was acquired from Edmonton last summer in a straight swap of highly-touted prospects, as Isaac Howard was sent to the Oilers. In 12 AHL games, O’Reilly has posted four points. He is a two-time Memorial Cup winner, and was the tournament’s MVP in 2026 with the Kitchener Rangers.



Injury Notes



Sabres defenseman Louis Crevier is a game-time decision for Wednesday’s game, according to Lindy Ruff. Meanwhile, goalie Alex Lyon will join Buffalo on its upcoming road trip as he works back from a shoulder injury, meaning it likely won’t be long before he makes his season debut.



As mentioned above, Tampa Bay will be missing a big piece in forward Brayden Point, who exited Sunday’s game against Winnipeg with an injury.

stories.title: Olen Zellweger Fitting Right In
stories.summary:
So, Who Is the Wonderful Wizard of Oz?



Olen Zellweger has been more than adequate since joining the Sabres. The hope was that he could at least partially fill the skates of the departed Bowen Byram, and for the most part, he’s done just that.



But who exactly is this young defenseman we’re still getting to know a little better with each passing game? Let us find out together.




Position: Defenseman



Shoots: Left



Height: 5’10”



Weight: Approximately 192 lbs



Born: September 10, 2003 Calgary, Alberta



Team: Buffalo Sabres



Drafted: 2021, 2nd round, 34th overall by Anaheim



Acquired: For Anton Wahlberg and a second-round draft pick



Age: 23




Back in June of this year, Buffalo acquired Zellweger from Anaheim in exchange for forward prospect Anton Wahlberg and a second-round pick in the 2026 NHL Draft, which the Ducks used to select Jayden Kurtz. The Sabres were looking to add a young defenseman with good skating ability, puck-moving skills, and offensive upside. Zellweger checked all those boxes and appeared to be a good fit for what Buffalo needed.



He is also under an affordable contract, signed by Buffalo through the 2028-29 season, carrying an annual salary cap hit of $3.1 million. He will be a restricted free agent then.



Olen is one of the more intriguing defensemen to join the Buffalo Sabres in recent years. He’s is a bit undersized but is an exceptionally mobile, offensively gifted defender whose skating and puck-moving abilities make him an exciting addition to Buffalo’s blue line. And have I mentioned his speed yet? He’s one of the faster defensemen in the NHL and has the ability to join the rush, carry the puck through the neutral zone and create offensive opportunities.



I used the term “Bo Byram-lite” when we acquired him this past summer and he really does share many of the same qualities. He’s not a stay-at-home defenseman. His game is built around mobility, puck possession and generating offense.



His greatest contributions will likely come from his ability to move the puck and help drive play, but that doesn’t mean he can’t hold his own defensively. We’ve seen him clear the crease this season, so he’s certainly not afraid to get physical in front of his own net. He just doesn’t have the size to do it consistently. Olen relies more on his skating ability and quickness to close gaps and get on attacking players before they have time to make a play. He has also added some bulk over the past few seasons, currently weighing in at 192 pounds compared to just 180 pounds three seasons ago.







Zellweger has shown offensive ability at virtually every level. He was a highly productive junior defenseman with the WHL’s Everett Silvertips and Kamloops Blazers. Some of his past accomplishments include:



Two-time WHL Defenseman of the Year (2022 and 2023).



2023 CHL Defenseman of the Year.



Two-time World Junior Championship gold medalist with Canada (2022 and 2023).



Recorded 37 points in 44 AHL games during his first professional season.



Now 23 years old, Zellweger played parts of three seasons with the Ducks before Buffalo acquired him. He compiled 16 goals and 35 assists for 51 points in 164 games. That’s pretty respectable production for a young defenseman just finding his footing in the NHL. The Sabres believe there’s considerably more offense to unlock, however. Olen has the potential to develop into a productive, middle-pairing offensive defenseman capable of consistently putting up 30–40 points per season, perhaps even more as his game continues to mature.



Zellweger has gotten off to a very encouraging start in Buffalo, and the early returns suggest the Sabres may have found exactly what they were looking for when they acquired him. He’s been receiving mostly positive reviews while averaging nearly 20 minutes of ice time per game and stepping into an elevated role on Buffalo’s blue line, playing primarily alongside Owen Power.



Offensively, he’s been productive as well. Zellweger has recorded 3 goals and 3 assists for 6 points in 16 games, putting him on a scoring pace that exceeds his production from last season in Anaheim. That includes an impressive two-goal performance against Montreal and a game-winning goal against San Jose.



Perhaps just as encouraging is the confidence the coaching staff has shown in him. He’s been trusted with meaningful minutes and an opportunity to contribute alongside Buffalo’s former number one overall pick. For a 23-year-old defenseman still developing his game, that’s a pretty significant vote of confidence.



The early returns have been promising. Zellweger possesses the offensive instincts, skating ability and puck-moving skills to become a valuable contributor on Buffalo’s blue line. If he continues to develop defensively and becomes more comfortable in his new surroundings, the Sabres could have themselves a dependable, productive second-pairing defenseman for the long term.



The biggest question is whether Zellweger can round out his game and become a reliable two-way NHL defenseman without sacrificing the offensive instincts that make him such an intriguing addition. If he can put it all together, Buffalo may have found a very nice piece for its defensive core.

stories.title: Sabres Vanquished by Knights, Lose 4-1 at Home
stories.summary:
Score: Buffalo Sabres 1, Vegas Golden Knights 4



Shots: Buffalo 28, Vegas 26



Sabres Goals: Malenstyn (Kozak);



Knights Goals: Marner (Unassisted); Eichel (Barbashev); Hertl (Marner); Hertl (2) (Barbashev, Theodore)



Summary



The Buffalo Sabres (8-6-3) fell 4-1 to the Vegas Golden Knights (12-5-2) at KeyBank Center on Sunday afternoon. Jack Eichel continued to terrorize the Sabres, scoring his seventh goal in eight games against his old team, while Tomas Hertl netted two to lead the Knights to victory. Despite the score, the Sabres came out ahead on the expected goals charts, but were unable to finish, especially in a particularly strong first period.



First Period: A Scoreless Frenzy



The first few chances of the period went the way of the home squad, as the Krebs-Thompson-Benson line worked a low cycle, getting the puck in front of the net , though Vegas was able to defend any really dangerous scoring chances. That line would go back to work just moments later, as Benson just missed a cross-ice redirection from Krebs that would have given the Sabres an early lead. Josh Doan then had a shot from the slot, but a defender’s stick kept the puck away from Vegas goalie Adin Hill. Despite these chances, the Sabres did not register a shot in the first five minutes of the game. 



Moments before the halfway mark of the period, the Sabres once again found some glorious chances, as Josh Norris hit Jiri Kulich with a slick feed to set up a 2-on-1 rush. Kulich opted to fire the puck, beating Hill but not the goalpost to keep the game scoreless. Just after that, the top line got back to work, shooting a puck just wide. Any further pressure was quelled, however, as Olen Zellweger took an offensive zone high sticking penalty to give the Knights a power play.



Based on the first minute, it was actually hard to tell which team had the man advantage however. Beck Malenstyn killed the first 20 seconds with a one man power kill in the Vegas zone, then Noah Östlund found himself with a breakaway, picking the pocket of Jack Eichel, that Hill was able to keep out of the net. On the couple occasions Vegas did enter the Sabres zone, they didn’t really take up any real estate there, managing no shots in the two minute man advantage. 



Hill had to make another save once each team returned to five aside, having to dive over to make a robbery with the glove, and it would continue to be a busy period for him. Malenstyn brought his a-game in the first period, being an absolute menace on the forecheck, almost leading to Sam Carrick burying his first of the season, but the Sabres couldn’t cleanly find the puck on a scramble out in front. 



Ellis did not face much of a test in the first period, but he did have to make one big save in the last few minutes, coming cross-crease to square up a Knights shot. Maybe off that chance though, Vegas found their most life of the period at the end, drawing another penalty, with Connor Timmins taking a high sticking penalty, though this call was incredibly dubious at best. 



The Sabres had yet another impressive penalty kill, and then an absolute flurry of chances at the end of the period, as Timmins brought the puck across the blue line after getting out the box to help initiative a sequence where Benson, Thompson, and Krebs all had fabulous opportunities but just could not get a puck by Adin Hill. Though the score of the period was non-existent, it was not for lack of effort. The Sabres held the edge in shots 15-6, despite having to kill two penalties, and the xG edge fell in the Sabres’ favor, 1.57 to 0.44. 



Second Period: Role Reversal



Though Vegas had an early push in the second period, with Eichel getting denied by Ellis on a one-timer, the Sabres kept up the pressure. Jack Quinn found himself with a glorious look taking the puck to the slot, but Hill was just able to get the blocker on it to keep the game scoreless. This pressure would give the Sabres their first chance of the game on the power play. 



The best chance of the power play once again went for the team who was a man down, as William Karlsson found himself with a clean breakaway off an errant pass from Tage Thompson. Ellis was able to make the first save, and despite not really knowing where the rebound was, got the pad over to stop the second one. It was a classic Ellis save, in that it looked awkward but it got the job done. 




Ellis save on Karlsson SH breakaway #LetsGoBuffalo #VegasBorn pic.twitter.com/5QjlRcUuiJ— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) November 8, 2026




While unsuccessful at recording the game’s first tally on their first power play, the Sabres got another opportunity just seconds after the first one expired, though this one had the same result as the first one, without needing Ellis to bail them out this time, though. 



Mattias Samuelsson had one of the better defensive highlights on the game, as the Knights came in on a rush, getting the puck to the slot, but they skated right into Sammy’s office, as he was able to swiftly knock the puck away. It’s Samuelsson’s bread and butter play and part of what makes him so invaluable to the team. 



The Sabres really fell out of rhythm in the back half of the second period, as they struggled to even escape their own zone. They weren’t allowing any opportunities that were too dangerous, and the ones they did get were turned away by Ellis, but the gap in shot differential closed quickly. 



The Sabres would get their third chance on the power play of the period, as Thompson was hooked carrying the puck up the ice with just over eight minutes to go in the period, and a team would indeed score on this one, though as was the trend, it was the team down a man. A Thompson pass at the blue line was deflected by Mitch Marner, who found himself all alone on Ellis, beating him on a backhand-forehand move, tapping the puck into an empty net to give the Knights a 1-0 lead with 7:42 to go in the period. 




Mitchell Marner, 1-0 SHG #LetsGoBuffalo #VegasBorn pic.twitter.com/CCdhAru6DV— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) November 8, 2026




As the power play expired, the Vegas offense didn’t. Power got outworked in the corner by Ivan Barbashev, who found Buffalo fan favorite Eichel all alone in front, easily able to bury it past Ellis for a 2-0 lead, just 1:30 after Marner made it 1-0. 




Jack Eichel gives the fans a little extra after scoring, 2-0 #LetsGoBuffalo #VegasBorn pic.twitter.com/7wgLssVRiA— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) November 8, 2026




The second period wound down with minimal fanfare, but the Knights completely flipped the script on the Sabres from the first period. Vegas outshot the Sabres 11-3 in the period, despite the Sabres being the team with three power plays, with the Sabres stills holding the xG edge, 2.45 to 2.1. 



Third Period:



To start the third, the first period Sabres made an appearance, with Connor Timmins getting the best look for his first goal as a Sabre, having a wide open net from a very sharp angle that he couldn’t bury, hitting the side of the post. 



FInally though, the Sabres got rewarded for their pressure. The fourth line went to work, as a mad scrum broke out in front of the net. There were seven total players around Hill in the crease, the puck squeaked loose and Tyson Kozak was there to slide it past Hill, though it apparently hit Malenstyn on the way in, to cut the lead to 2-1 with 15 minutes left in the game.








Not sure who will get credited with this goal, but Buffalo pulls within one after crease chaos, 2-1#LetsGoBuffalo #VegasBorn pic.twitter.com/Z3bpvdaO15— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) November 8, 2026




Right after cutting the lead in half, Ellis was tested to keep it there, and was up to the task, stopping Marner in front. The Sabres then kept the puck in the zone for a full shift, headlined by Dahlin and Power, but at the end of the shift, with Power gassed, Tomas Hertl danced around him, beating Ellis over the top shoulder to give the Knights’ their two goal lead right back, just 1:15 after the Sabres scored.




Brutal from the Sabres.  Hertl, 3-1 #LetsGoBuffalo #VegasBorn pic.twitter.com/jSmqebsrs9— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) November 8, 2026




The fourth line had another chance to cut the lead back to one, but Carrick got robbed in the slot by Hill to keep the two goal lead with 13 minutes left. 



Unfortunately for the Sabres, Hertl was not done scoring yet. At exactly 10 minutes left to go in the period, Hertl found himself alone in front of Ellis, once again making no mistake, this time beating him clean on a wrister over the shoulder, extending the Vegas lead to 4-1. 




Hertl's second goal of the game, 4-1#LetsGoBuffalo #VegasBorn pic.twitter.com/J1tV5vOgJ2— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) November 8, 2026




The fourth goal took all the life out of the Sabres for, who went from attacking most of the game to incredibly passive after falling behind by three. There was a sequence of nice looks with around five minutes left, as Dahlin, Quinn, and Östlund all had some nice chances that either deflected wide or were stopped by Hill. Moments later, Ellis robbed Eichel of his second of the game on a cross-ice feed. Ellis then robbed William Karlsson in front of the net with just over three minutes to go. The Sabres were forced to kill off one last penalty at the end, and did so successfully, keeping the final score at 4-1. 



Conclusion



Despite a slight edge in shots, 28-26, and xG, 3.54-3.46, the Sabres could not find a way to get a puck past Adin Hill, and Vegas was able to coast home in the back half of the third period. Ellis finished a slight negative in goals saved above expected, and while he was pretty strong overall with a lot of nice saves, he couldn’t give the Sabres the big save to keep them in the game. 




NHL Game Score Impact Card for Buffalo Sabres on 2026-11-08: pic.twitter.com/4R3lXyRWrU— HockeyStatCards (@hockeystatcards) November 8, 2026




Other Notes



The Power Play continues to be a bugaboo for the Sabres. Even though it looked like it was turning a corner after the Kings game to end the road trip, they have not scored a goal since then, though their opportunities have looked a bit better. In this game it was actively detrimental for them. Something has to be done to get actual results and not just moral victories. Perhaps a few more pages should be added to the dossier.



We’ll see if Ryan McLeod and Louis Crevier draw back into the lineup, there is potential for a couple spots in the lineup to shake free after the loss. Zach Metsa was the lone defenseman to play under 15 minutes in the game, with Connor Timmins in his second game back from injury logging a good amount of ice time and realistically playing well through those two games. Despite always seeming to stay in the lineup, he never logs a ton of minutes and Crevier had enough expectations heading into the season that the Sabres will want to get him going.



For McLeod to come back in, there are a few options. Considering that the fourth line mustered the only goal and have been playing respectably, that may not be the card that Ruff decides to play to get McLeod back in. Rather he may look to McLeod’s inverse jersey number, as Jason Zucker has looked quite slow coming off sports hernia surgery. At age 34, we can’t be sure if Zucker is actually done or if he’s struggling to acclimate after a notoriously finnicky surgery. Either way, McLeod could slot back in on the wing for him, or potentially even for Jiri Kulich, who took an ill-advised shot that led to the second goal for Vegas, and logged just over 10 minutes of ice time in the game. 



If there is one positive in the game for the Sabres, it was the penalty kill, who had a perfect evening and often times made the Vegas power play, which is typically dangerous, look ineffective in the game. The struggles of the Sabres PK have been heavily documented to start the season but it appears they may be turning the corner. 



What’s Next?



The Sabres next take the ice at home on Wednesday night, where they will host the Tampa Bay Lightning for the first time this season. Following that, they will hit the road for a six game trip, the first game of which happens the following night, where they will travel to Chicago to face the Blackhawks.

stories.title: Game #16 Preview & Open Thread: Sabres vs Golden Knights
stories.summary:
Buffalo gets another measuring-stick game against the defending Western Conference champions



Vegas Golden Knights (11-5-2) at Buffalo Sabres (8-5-3)



Puck Drop: 3:30 p.m. ET | KeyBank Center, Buffalo, NYTV: MSG-B, Scripps, SN1, TVASStreaming: DAZN in the Sabres marketRadio: WGR 550 / Buffalo Sabres App



The Sabres finally put together the kind of game they have been searching for on Friday. Now comes the harder part. Do it again against one of the best teams in the Western Conference.



Buffalo welcomes the reigning Western Conference champion Vegas Golden Knights to KeyBank Center today after beating Columbus 5-2 in one of its most complete performances of the season. Josh Norris scored twice, Owen Power tied his career high with three assists, and Buffalo controlled large portions of the game rather than spending the night trying to erase another deficit.



The win improved Buffalo to 8-5-3 and gives the Sabres a chance to make it five wins in six games. Vegas presents a considerably different challenge. The Golden Knights arrive at 11-5-2, sit second in the Pacific Division and are 2-0-1 on their current road trip. All three games have been decided by one goal. If Buffalo wants to prove the recent stretch represents more than just a hot week, this is a pretty good place to start.



Know Your Opponent



Vegas Golden Knights



Record: 11-5-2 | 24 PTSDivision: 2nd, PacificLast Game: 2-1 win at DetroitRoad Trip: 2-0-1Last Season vs. Buffalo: 0-2-0



Jack Eichel. Mark Stone. Mitch Marner. Tomas Hertl. William Karlsson.



Eichel returns to Buffalo with 23 points in 18 games, including seven goals and 16 assists. Stone has 19 points, Marner has 18 and Hertl has 12. Rookie Trevor Connelly has scored in three consecutive games and enters today tied for the rookie scoring lead with 12 points. His seven goals rank second among NHL rookies. He also reached a top skating speed of 23.73 mph earlier this season, fifth-fastest in the league at the time. Load up against Eichel and Stone and the Karlsson-Marner line can hurt you. Survive the top six and Hertl and Connelly are waiting on the third line. There aren’t many easy shifts.



What to Watch



1. Can Buffalo Build Off Its Best Game?



Friday’s win over Columbus felt different. Buffalo didn’t need a miracle comeback. They didn’t spend the entire game scrambling to repair mistakes, they just played well.



The Sabres outskated Columbus, generated offense from multiple lines and got the kind of goaltending they needed from Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen in the 5-2 victory. That sounds simple, but consistency has been the challenge.



Buffalo is 4-1-0 over its last five games, and its goaltenders have combined for a .916 save percentage since Oct. 27, fourth-best in the NHL over that span. 



The Sabres don’t need to reinvent anything against Vegas. Get pucks behind the defense. Win battles. Don’t force offense through the middle of the ice. Make Vegas defend for entire shifts. Because if Buffalo starts turning pucks over and trading chances with this team, Vegas has enough finishers to turn the game quickly.



2. Jack Eichel Is Back in Buffalo



Here we go again. There will probably never be a Sabres-Golden Knights game in Buffalo where Jack Eichel isn’t one of the main storylines. But this time the focus should probably be less about the history and more about how good Eichel currently is. He leads Vegas with 23 points in 18 games and has picked up three assists over his last two games. Eichel is expected to center Brett Howden and Mark Stone, giving Vegas a first line with size, skill and the ability to dominate possession below the circles. That should create a heavyweight matchup for Rasmus Dahlin and Mattias Samuelsson.



Buffalo has done a good job against Eichel’s Golden Knights recently. The Sabres swept Vegas last season, winning 3-2 at KeyBank Center and then shutting out the Golden Knights 2-0 in Las Vegas two weeks later. Do it again and Buffalo will have earned it.



3. Dahlin Hits 600



Today is another milestone for Rasmus Dahlin. The Sabres captain is set to play his 600th NHL game, becoming the 17th player to reach 600 games in a Buffalo uniform. And Buffalo will need him. Vegas has too many lines capable of creating offense for Dahlin to have an easy matchup. Expect him and Samuelsson to see plenty of Eichel and Stone, while Dahlin will also be responsible for helping Buffalo break Vegas’ forecheck and get clean exits. This is the type of game where Buffalo needs its captain to look like its captain.



4. Don’t Forget About Trevor Connelly



Vegas didn’t exactly need another dangerous forward. But, Trevor Connelly has goals in three straight games, including Thursday’s game-winner against Detroit with only 1:42 remaining in regulation. His emergence has changed the construction of Vegas’ lineup. Instead of needing to load its best players together, the Golden Knights can put Connelly alongside Tomas Hertl on a third line and create a matchup problem against teams whose defensive depth isn’t strong enough. That will put pressure on Buffalo’s Power-Zellweger pairing and on a third defensive pair that is expected to feature Zach Metsa and Conor Timmins. Timmins made his season debut Friday and immediately contributed an assist and two blocked shots while logging more than three minutes on the penalty kill. Against Vegas, Buffalo can’t have one defensive pairing merely survive. All three need to hold up.



5. Benson and Thompson Keep Rolling



Don’t overlook what’s happening with Zach Benson. Benson enters today riding a career-best six-game point streak, collecting two goals and seven assists during that stretch. His 13 assists lead Buffalo. (NHL) Tage Thompson has quietly put together his own streak. Thompson has points in five straight games and leads Buffalo with 18 points and 10 goals this season. (NHL) Putting Benson and Thompson together with Peyton Krebs gives Buffalo a line that can play several different ways. Thompson can obviously shoot.



Benson retrieves pucks and creates plays in tight areas.



Krebs can bring pressure through the middle and help get Thompson the puck rather than forcing Tage to generate everything himself.



Against Vegas’ depth, Buffalo needs that line to drive offense rather than merely cancel out Eichel’s group.



Projected Lineups



Buffalo Sabres



Forwards



Zach Benson – Peyton Krebs – Tage ThompsonJosh Doan – Noah Östlund – Jack QuinnJiri Kulich – Josh Norris – Jason ZuckerBeck Malenstyn – Tyson Kozak – Sam Carrick



Defense



Rasmus Dahlin – Mattias SamuelssonOlen Zellweger – Owen PowerZach Metsa – Conor Timmins



Goaltenders



Colten EllisUkko-Pekka Luukkonen



Expected starter: Colten Ellis



Ellis had the starter’s net at Saturday’s practice, which typically indicates he’ll get the start. He owns a .909 save percentage over his last three starts. 



Expected scratches: Ryan McLeod, Louis Crevier



Injured: Konsta Helenius, Justin Danforth, Matt Grzelcyk, Alex Lyon. 



Vegas Golden Knights



Forwards



Brett Howden – Jack Eichel – Mark StoneIvan Barbashev – William Karlsson – Mitch MarnerTrevor Connelly – Tomas Hertl – Victor OlofssonBraeden Bowman – Nic Dowd – Marc Gatcomb



Defense



Brayden McNabb – Shea TheodoreJeremy Lauzon – Rasmus AnderssonNoah Hanifin – Dylan Coghlan



Goaltenders



Adin HillCarter Hart



Expected starter: Adin Hill



NHL.com’s latest projection lists Hill as the likely change in goal after Carter Hart started Vegas’ 2-1 victory in Detroit. (NHL)



Expected scratch: Raphael Lavoie



Injured: Parker Wotherspoon. (NHL)



One More Thing: Buffalo Has Owned the Pacific



Maybe this matchup isn’t as intimidating to Buffalo as it looks.



Since the beginning of last season, the Sabres are 16-2-1 against Pacific Division teams, good for an .868 points percentage.



That stretch includes Buffalo’s recent sweep through California and last season’s sweep of Vegas. (NHL)



That’s not a tiny one-week run anymore.



Buffalo has consistently matched up well against teams from the Pacific.



Today would be a pretty good time to continue it.



Final Thoughts



The Sabres have spent the opening month of the season trying to establish exactly what kind of team they are.



Vegas should help answer the question.



The Golden Knights are deep.



They’re experienced.



They have elite talent at the top of the lineup and one of the league’s more dangerous rookies giving them even more depth.



And they’re coming into Buffalo as the defending Western Conference champions.



This is exactly the type of opponent the Sabres need to start beating consistently if they want to be taken seriously as something more than a team fighting for the final playoff spots.



Buffalo doesn’t need another dramatic comeback.



It doesn’t need overtime.



It doesn’t need a moral victory.



Play the way it did against Columbus.



Get Thompson and Benson involved early. Make Eichel defend. Don’t give Vegas’ third line favorable matchups. Let Dahlin control the game in his 600th appearance.



And find out whether Friday’s performance was one good night — or the beginning of Buffalo becoming the team it believes it can be.

stories.title: Sabres Slice and Dice the Jackets
stories.summary:
Buffalo Bounces Back Bigtime with Inspired Effort



Score: Buffalo Sabres 5-2 Columbus Blue JacketsShots: BUF 37-26 COL



Buffalo Sabres Goals: Quinn 9th (Power, Timmins) Norris 3rd (Power) Dahlin 3rd (Krebs, Power) Norris 4th (Benson, Thompson) Doan 3rd (Östlund, Quinn)Columbus Blue Jackets Goals: Johnson 8th (Monahan, Mateychuk) Werenski 2nd (Knies, Johnson)



Plus 1: Power’s Play



Buffalo came out fast and furious, taking the fight to the Blue Jackets’ defense. The Sabres forechecked hard, generated several scoring chances, and drew the game’s first penalty when Damon Severson was called for tripping Zach Benson. Buffalo had a few good looks on the power play but couldn’t get the puck past Columbus netminder Jet Greaves.



The Sabres continued to keep the pressure on, recording 11 shot attempts in just the first seven minutes of play. On a nice rush, Owen Power dished the puck to Jack Quinn, who carried it into the slot and fired a shot that was stopped by Greaves. Quinn stayed with it, however, pounced on the rebound and buried it with a backhand for his ninth goal of the season. Buffalo was dominating early, holding a commanding 6-0 advantage in shots at that point.



Columbus eventually began to wake up and put together a few good shifts. Quinn then made his presence felt at the other end of the ice, tying up a Blue Jackets player while Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen was down and out, with half the net empty. A great defensive effort by number 22.



The Blue Jackets would tie things up at the 16:00 mark. Kent Johnson fired home a shot after receiving a slick pass from Sean Monahan behind the goal line in the corner. Buffalo’s fourth line had been trapped on the ice for a lengthy shift of about a minute and a half, and with Columbus cycling the puck, a breakdown seemed inevitable.



The Sabres would answer with a huge late-period goal of their own. The struggling Josh Norris, who could just as easily have found himself scratched like linemate Ryan McLeod, would come up big. It started with a turnover at center ice, where Owen Power chipped the puck ahead to Norris. He carried it over the blue line before cutting toward the middle, showing tremendous patience as he looked for his opportunity. Meanwhile, Jack Quinn headed to the net, drawing the attention of the other defender. Norris used defenseman Ivan Provorov as a screen and slipped the puck past the goaltender to give Buffalo a 2-1 lead. Two assists for Owen in the period.







Plus 2: Columbus Cannonballed



Buffalo took an unnecessary too-many-men-on-the-ice penalty early, forcing the penalty kill into action. Thankfully, the Sabres managed to kill it off, despite an egregious turnover in front of Luukkonen with just seconds remaining that nearly proved costly.



The Sabres would turn that close call into a goal shortly afterward. Following a battle along the boards, Peyton Krebs worked the puck back to Owen Power, who quickly moved it cross-ice to Rasmus Dahlin. The Captain unleashed a slap shot from the point that eluded Greaves, giving the home team a 3-1 lead. Excellent board work by Krebs to win possession, and Power’s cross-ice feed marked his third helper of the evening.



Buffalo continued to apply the pressure, and Josh Norris was rewarded with his second goal of the night. Tage Thompson showed off his stickhandling skills, protecting the puck near the blue line before sending it along the boards and behind the net to Zach Benson. Taz wasted no time, firing a quick pass out front to Norris, who made a slick move and tucked the puck past a sprawling Jet Greaves.



It was a huge goal for the beleaguered forward, giving Buffalo a commanding 4-1 lead and hopefully providing Norris with a much-needed confidence boost.



But we weren’t done yet, folks! Josh Doan joined in on the fun, credited with a goal that pinballed in off his body. Doan was once again doing what he does best, getting to the net, where he spent much of the evening. This time, however, he was right in the crease, prompting Columbus to challenge the goal for goaltender interference.



After review, the officials determined that the contact was minimal and did not prevent Jet Greaves from making the save. The goal would stand. Credit Jack Quinn with a big assist, as he skated out from behind the net while being shadowed, spun around and fired a shot toward the goal. The puck tipped off Noah Östlund before finding Doan, who picked up his third of the season.



Both Josh’s needed to get those monkeys off their backs, and both came through in a big way. Buffalo continued to dominate, piling up a whopping 33 shots on net through two periods while building a commanding 5-1 lead. The Sabres were firing on all cylinders, keeping the pressure on Columbus and putting themselves in a terrific position heading into the third.



Plus 3: Jackets Sent to the Cleaners



Luukkonen was tested with a few early shots and looked sharp, turning them aside. He had a strong game overall. The Blue Jackets were playing the second half of a back-to-back, but they weren’t going away quietly. Still, the Sabres did a good job limiting their opportunities, as Columbus managed just four shots through the first eight minutes of the period.



Buffalo’s offense understandably slowed down, but it wasn’t a return to the offensive ineptitude we’ve seen at times this season. With a commanding lead, the Sabres played a responsible third period, managed the game well, and didn’t give Columbus much room to get back into it.



Unfortunately, the Blue Jackets would get a late power-play goal after Tyson Kozak was called for tripping. That would be the final goal of the night, with Buffalo coming away with a convincing 5-2 victory.



A much-needed win for the Sabres after failing to hold their lead against Ottawa the other night. This time, there would be no late collapse. Buffalo played the third period the RIGHT WAY, protecting its lead, limiting Columbus’ opportunities, and seeing the game through to the final horn. That’s exactly the kind of response you want to see from this team.



Owen Power led the way for Buffalo with three assists in the game. However, Josh Norris was an absolute beast in this contest, seemingly everywhere on the ice. It sure looks like he received the wake-up call he needed. Jack Quinn was a force as well, opening the scoring and finishing the night with two points.



This was a tremendous team effort from top to bottom. Matthew Knies and Adam Fantilli couldn’t find much room behind the Buffalo defense and were largely kept quiet throughout the game. Conor Timmins was solid in his first appearance of the season, even picking up an assist on Quinn’s goal. And just as an observation, Beck Malenstyn’s shot-blocking is nothing short of epic. The guy seems to be throwing himself in front of everything, and he does it consistently.



Photo Credits: Sabres.com, X.com









Final Thoughts:



The Sabres partnered with Roswell Park for Hockey Fights Cancer Night, highlighting the inspiring story of young Eddie Golden and his courageous battle with leukemia. Eddie’s story was shared with fans on the jumbotron before the youngster got a special opportunity to drop the ceremonial puck alongside his favorite Sabres player, Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen. A memorable moment for Eddie and everyone in attendance. He was even named First Star of the game.







Keep fighting, Eddie! We’re all rooting for you!



With the return of Juri Kulich to the lineup, Ryan McLeod was scratched for the first time in his Buffalo tenure. (and for his career). McLeod has managed just one goal and three points through 15 games with the Sabres this season. His defensive game has also been slipping for some time now. Perhaps a spell in the press box will do the two-time 50-point scorer some good and help get him back on track.



Louis Crevier also sat this one out as Conor Timmins made his long-awaited return to the lineup. Timmins had been sidelined since the start of the season while recovering from a lower-body injury suffered during the preseason. He’s one of the better penalty-killing defensemen on Buffalo’s roster, so his return should provide a welcome boost to one of the Sabres’ problem areas.



Next up, the Sabres continue the homestand at KeyBank Center on Sunday, November 8th, hosting the Vegas Golden Knights at 3:30 pm. Making his return to Buffalo will be old friend, old nemesis, and recently resurrected undead Jack Eichel.

stories.title: Davison Igbinosun: The draft day hate was way overblown
stories.summary:
A lot of folks on here were losing their minds when we drafted Davison Igbinosun, and honestly, the reaction was way overly critical.



	 



	I get where the frustration came from initially. If you watched him at Ohio State, the grabby play and the flags would drive fans batty. But look at the actual body of work—the guy put up great stats, and more importantly, his penalties dropped off dramatically in his final college season once he dialed in the technique.



	 



	Everything we’ve seen out of camp and preseason tells me this kid is a pure competitor. Is he going to get flagged sometimes as a rookie? Probably. Is he going to take some lumps adjusting to NFL receivers? Almost certainly. But what you are getting is pure nastiness, legitimate toughness, and a guy who flat out refuses to back down from anyone. He’s got the ideal physical traits and he’s ridiculously sticky in press-man.



	 



	I mentioned this in another thread, but his real value is going to show up on high-leverage downs. When we dial up a blitz on 3rd-and-medium and the DC needs corners who can get in a receiver's face, disrupt the timing, and hold up on an island for 2.2 seconds to let the rush get home, Igbinosun is built for that exact role.



	 



	Yeah, it's just preseason, but you can't teach that kind of edge. I really like what I'm seeing from him so far.
